questions.q: Write the equation that links density, mass and volume.
Name the change of state from a gas to a liquid.
What happens to the temperature of a substance while it is changing state?
questions.a: It stays the same (the energy goes into breaking bonds, not raising the temperature)

questions.q: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?

questions.a: The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in a system

questions.q: Why does a gas exert a pressure on the walls of its container?
questions.a: Its particles collide with the walls and exert a force on them

rows.task: Draw a particle picture for a solid, liquid and gas. Under the diagrams write the names of the changes of state.
Coal, oil and gas are examples of solids, liquids and gases. Describe in words the arrangement of particles in a solid, liquid and gas.

Sketch a heating curve and label the sections. Use your book to help you if you are struggling. Go back to the calculation questions (e) and (f) and try them again. Make sure you put the numbers under the formula given to avoid mistakes.

Using your book or text book to help, rewrite the method for working out the density of an irregular shape. Make sure you state the equipment you use and what measurements you are taking. Do this in bullet points.
Draw a heating curve and label up the sections on the graph. What do the flat regions represent? What is happening to the kinetic and potential energy across the graph?
Write a step by step set of instructions that explains how you measure the density of an irregular object. Make sure you include the equipment you use and the measurements you take.
Define the specific heat capacity of a material. If the specific heat capacity is large, does it take a short time or long time to heat up? Why? Explain your answer.

In an experiment there are independent, dependent and control variables. What do each of these mean? Go back to Q4. Can you now identify these from the investigation? What does the word ‘accurate’ mean in an experiment? How is it different from the word ‘precise’. Explain your answer.

questions.q: The water in the kettle boiled for a short time before the kettle switched off. During this time 5.0 g of water changed to steam. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2 260 000 J/kg. Calculate the energy transferred to change the water to steam. Use the Physics Equations Sheet.

Calculate the energy transferred to the surroundings as 0.40 kg of stearic acid changed state from liquid to solid. The specific latent heat of fusion of stearic acid is 199 000 J / kg. Use the correct equation from the Physics Equations Sheet.
What is meant by specific latent heat of fusion?
questions.a: The amount of energy needed to change 1 kg (unit mass) of a substance from solid to liquid, with no change in temperature.

questions.q: The helium in the balloon has a mass of 0.00254 kg. The balloon has a volume of 0.0141 m^3. Calculate the density of helium. Choose the correct unit: m^3/kg, kg/m^3 or kg m^3.
The student only took one set of measurements to determine the density of the rock. Explain why taking the measurements more than once may improve the accuracy of the density value.
questions.a: A mean can be calculated, which reduces the effect of random errors.

questions.q: The mass of water in the kettle was 0.50 kg. The temperature of the water increased from 20 °C to 100 °C. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the water. Use the Physics Equations Sheet.

When the car engine is working normally, 2 kg of coolant passes through the radiator each second. The temperature of the coolant falls from 112 °C to 97 °C. Calculate the energy transferred each second from the coolant. Specific heat capacity of the coolant = 3800 J/kg °C.
What is meant by specific heat capacity?
questions.a: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg (unit mass) of a substance by 1 °C.

questions.q: Explain how the internal energy of the water changes as it is heated from 20 °C to 25 °C.
questions.a: The (mean) kinetic energy of the particles increases, which increases the internal energy of the water.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of particles, how evaporation causes the cooling of water.
questions.a: The fastest particles have enough energy to escape from the surface of the water. So the mean energy of the remaining particles decreases. The lower the mean energy of the particles, the lower the temperature of the water.
